# certstream-server-rust

> A Certificate Transparency log streaming server written in Rust. It monitors every Chrome- and Apple-trusted CT log and streams newly issued TLS certificates in real time over WebSocket and SSE. It speaks both RFC 6962 and the static-ct-api tile protocol from one binary, and is a drop-in replacement for certstream-server and certstream-server-go.

Typical uses: phishing and typosquat detection, brand monitoring, attack surface discovery, threat intelligence pipelines, certificate inventory, and research on newly issued certificates.

Throughput on a typical deployment: around 420 certificates and 700 domain names per second, roughly 36 million certificates and 62 million domain names per day, at about 80 MB resident memory and a fifth of one CPU core.

## Docs

- [Home](https://certstream.dev/): what the project is, install options, feature list
- [API documentation](https://certstream.dev/docs.html): WebSocket and SSE endpoints, message formats, environment variables, REST API
- [Quick start](https://certstream.dev/quickstart.html): running the server and connecting a first client
- [Architecture](https://certstream.dev/architecture.html): ingest pipeline, broadcast path, dedup, state persistence

## Engineering writing

- [Why jemalloc RSS is 4x the live heap](https://certstream.dev/blog/jemalloc-transparent-huge-pages-rss.html): diagnosing a 358 MB resident set against a 52 MB live heap, where transparent huge pages held 206 MB the allocator could not return, and the thp:never fix
- [Reading Certificate Transparency tiles without a checkpoint](https://certstream.dev/blog/ct-logs-tiles-without-checkpoint.html): CT logs that serve static-ct-api tiles but return 404 for /checkpoint, reading them with the tree size from get-sth, and the failures that only appear against live logs
- [HTTP/2 multiplexing vs per-connection rate limits](https://certstream.dev/blog/http2-multiplexing-vs-per-connection-rate-limits.html): measuring whether pinning an operator to HTTP/1.1 helps, why the connection count confirmed the mechanism but the throughput refuted the theory, and finding the real limit in what the server returns per request
